summary: This document specifies how to augment the Routing Policy Specification Language inetnum: class to point to geofeed data, which are CSV files stating where IP address ranges are located. It also describes an optional scheme using the Routing PKI to authenticate those files. It was replaced by RFC 9632.

eli5.summary: Network owners can publish a file saying which place each of their addresses is in. This document explains how to find that file and check it is genuine. It was replaced by RFC 9632.

questions: how to publish ip geolocation data rpsl
subtitle: Finding and publishing geolocation data for IP address ranges.

tldr.problem: Internet services and infrastructure want to publish which geographic locations their IP addresses are in, but there is no standard way to discover these geolocation files.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9092 specifies how to add a URL pointing to a geofeed file in the Routing Policy Specification Language inetnum database object, and optionally how to sign those files using RPKI certificates for authenticity.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now publish geolocation data that content providers can discover and verify, but this RFC was replaced by RFC 9632 with improvements.

facts.label: Optional signing
facts.value: RPKI certificates with CMS detached signatures

facts.label: Recommended fetch interval
facts.value: Weekly or per HTTP Expires header

today: RFC 9092 was a Proposed Standard published in July 2021. It has been obsoleted by RFC 9632, which supersedes it with improvements.

sections.title: Why Geolocation Matters
sections.content:
Internet content providers and network infrastructure operators want to customize their services based on where users and services are located. They determine location from the user's IP address. Geofeed is the name for a CSV file that maps IP address ranges to geographic locations.

RFC 8805 defined the format for these geofeed files, but did not specify how to find the right file given an IP address. RFC 9092 fills that gap by showing how network operators can register their geofeed files so that others can find them.
sections.eli5: When you visit a website from France, it might show you a French version. The site knows you are in France because it has a list of IP addresses and which countries they are in.

sections.title: How Geofeed Discovery Works
sections.content:
The Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL) is used by Regional Internet Registries to store data about IP address ranges. Each range has an inetnum object that records who owns it and other details.

RFC 9092 allows operators to add a reference to their geofeed file in the inetnum object, either as a remarks: Geofeed attribute or as a dedicated geofeed: attribute. Both point to an HTTPS URL where the geofeed CSV file lives. To find geolocation data for an IP address, a lookup tool searches the RPSL database for the most specific inetnum object covering that address, then fetches the geofeed file from the URL it contains.
sections.eli5: Imagine a phone book where each entry says 'Call this number to find where these addresses are.' The geofeed URL is like that phone number.

sections.title: Authenticating Geofeed Files
sections.content:
RPSL data in many registries is only weakly authenticated. An attacker could modify an inetnum object to point to a fake geofeed file with false location claims.

RFC 9092 defines an optional signature scheme using RPKI certificates. A geofeed file can be signed with a private key that corresponds to an RPKI certificate covering the IP ranges in the file. To verify the signature, the receiver fetches the certificate from the public RPKI and checks that it covers all the prefixes in the geofeed, that the signature is valid, and that the certificate chain is valid. The signature is appended to the CSV file as BASE64-encoded comments.
sections.eli5: You can prove the location file is real by signing it with a special key that the RPKI network trusts. It is like a tamper-evident seal on a letter.

sections.title: Practical Deployment
sections.content:
Geofeed files must be published and fetched using HTTPS for encryption and server authentication. Operators who want to register their geofeed location must coordinate with their Regional Internet Registry or other registry authority that manages their inetnum objects.

To prevent overloading registry and geofeed servers, RFC 9092 recommends that collectors not fetch geofeed data more than once a week, and should respect HTTP Expires headers that indicate when new data is available. Bulk access should use FTP or RDAP rather than WHOIS to minimize load.
sections.eli5: Use HTTPS so no one can tamper with the file. Only check for updates once a week, so the servers do not get tired.

sections.title: Privacy Implications
sections.content: Publishing geofeed data makes it easy for anyone to discover which locations own or operate particular IP address ranges. This information can reveal the approximate location of services or users, which may have privacy implications. RFC 9092 acknowledges that it makes bulk access to geolocation data easier than before, and operators who publish geofeed pointers should be aware of this exposure.
sections.eli5: If someone knows that IP addresses belong to a company, they can find out where the company's computers are. That might not be secret information the company wants to share.
